title: The Journey That Almost Took Everything

pages.text: For eighteen months after finishing senior high school, twenty-year-old Kwabena woke up at dawn to repair neighbours’ fans and irons on the veranda while applying for factory and office jobs. Some weeks he earned eighty cedis; other weeks, almost nothing. One rainy evening, his fourteen-year-old sister Afia saw him staring at a flashy phone video of a stranger posing beside a sports car in Europe.
sentences: For eighteen months after finishing senior high school, twenty-year-old Kwabena woke up at dawn to repair neighbours’ fans and irons on the veranda while applying for factory and office jobs.

One rainy evening, his fourteen-year-old sister Afia saw him staring at a flashy phone video of a stranger posing beside a sports car in Europe.
pages.alt: Twenty-year-old Kwabena sits on the veranda beside his small electrical repair toolkit, looking at a flashy video on his phone while fourteen-year-old Afia watches.

pages.text: ‘Look at this message, Afia,’ said Kwabena softly. ‘A man calling himself an international travel connection says that if our family sells Grandma’s cocoa plot and pays him thirty-five thousand cedis in cash by Friday, he will take me through an unverified route with no embassy interview and give me a hotel job paying twenty thousand cedis a month!’ Afia felt a chill of worry.
sentences: ‘Look at this message, Afia,’ said Kwabena softly.

‘A man calling himself an international travel connection says that if our family sells Grandma’s cocoa plot and pays him thirty-five thousand cedis in cash by Friday, he will take me through an unverified route with no embassy interview and give me a hotel job paying twenty thousand cedis a month!’ Afia felt a chill of worry.
pages.alt: Kwabena shows Afia a hurried text message demanding 35,000 cedis in cash with no official visa or contract.

pages.text: When Kwabena told their parents at supper, Maame looked torn between worry and hope. ‘Many families sacrifice so a child can travel and help those at home,’ she said quietly. ‘Wanting a better life or travelling abroad is never shameful or unpatriotic. People migrate for education, work and family support all over the world. The question we must ask is whether this offer is truthful and safe!’

pages.alt: Around the family supper table, Maame speaks calmly with Kwabena and Afia about making informed, safe choices.

pages.text: Afia opened her JHS Computing and Social Studies notebook. ‘Before anyone pays thirty-five thousand cedis, let us verify three facts,’ she said. ‘First, is this agent licensed by the Ghana Immigration Service or the Labour Department? Second, does the country he named allow work without an official embassy visa? Third, can we check the company name?’ When they searched the official registry, the agent’s company did not exist at all!

pages.alt: Afia and Kwabena check the official government registry on a laptop and discover the agent’s company is not registered.

pages.text: The next morning, Maame asked Kwabena and Afia to visit Uncle Tetteh at his busy electrical and solar workshop near the market. Five years earlier, Uncle Tetteh had believed a similar smuggler’s promise. Sitting beside his workbench, Uncle Tetteh spoke without shame or exaggeration, only quiet truth.
sentences: The next morning, Maame asked Kwabena and Afia to visit Uncle Tetteh at his busy electrical and solar workshop near the market.
Five years earlier, Uncle Tetteh had believed a similar smuggler’s promise.
Sitting beside his workbench, Uncle Tetteh spoke without shame or exaggeration, only quiet truth.
pages.alt: In a bright solar-and-electrical workshop, Uncle Tetteh sits with Kwabena and Afia to share his real experience.

pages.text: ‘The smuggler took my family’s thirty thousand cedis and promised a direct flight,’ Uncle Tetteh explained. ‘Instead, we were abandoned at a transit stop with fake papers, stranded without legal rights to work, and forced into unpaid labour until a humanitarian return programme helped us come home safely. Smugglers and traffickers profit from secrecy and false photos. They never show the debt, the danger, or the legal traps.’

pages.alt: Uncle Tetteh points to a travel safety poster warning against fake visas, debt bondage and unlicensed smugglers.

pages.text: That evening, the family arranged a video call with their cousin Sister Akua, who worked legally as a registered nurse in the United Kingdom. ‘Travelling abroad legally is completely different from using a smuggler,’ Sister Akua told Kwabena warmly. ‘I completed my nursing qualification in Ghana, passed my official exams, signed a verified hospital contract, and obtained a work visa directly through the embassy.’
sentences: That evening, the family arranged a video call with their cousin Sister Akua, who worked legally as a registered nurse in the United Kingdom.

pages.alt: On a tablet video call, cousin Akua in nursing scrubs explains how she migrated legally with verified qualifications and an official visa.

pages.text: ‘And let me be honest with you, Kwabena,’ Sister Akua added with a gentle smile. ‘Life abroad is not money growing on trees! I work long shifts, pay high rent, heating bills and taxes in winter, and budget carefully before sending remittances home. Whether you work abroad legally or build a career in Ghana, real success always requires certified skills, legal status and hard work.’

pages.alt: Sister Akua holds up a monthly budget pie chart showing rent, taxes, bills and savings alongside her nursing study books.

pages.text: Kwabena looked down at the thirty-five-thousand-cedi figure in Afia’s notebook. ‘If we do not give our family’s savings to a fraudster,’ he asked Uncle Tetteh the next day, ‘what can a young person actually build right here?’ Uncle Tetteh smiled and pointed to the solar inverters and cold-room panels queued up in his workshop. ‘We have a shortage of certified solar and industrial electrical technicians right here in our district!’

‘We have a shortage of certified solar and industrial electrical technicians right here in our district!’
pages.alt: Uncle Tetteh shows Kwabena a row of solar inverters and control panels waiting to be installed for local farms and clinics.

pages.text: Together with his parents, Kwabena made a realistic, numbers-based plan. Instead of selling Grandma’s cocoa plot to pay thirty-five thousand cedis to a scammer, the family kept their land and invested four thousand five hundred cedis of saved capital: two thousand five hundred cedis for Kwabena’s accredited six-month solar-electrical certification at the technical institute, and two thousand cedis for professional diagnostic tools.

pages.alt: Kwabena, Afia and their parents write a 4,500-cedi training-and-tools investment plan while keeping the family cocoa farm intact.

pages.text: Kwabena studied hard, earned his national technical certificate, and partnered with Uncle Tetteh to wire solar water pumps and backup power for clinics, poultry farms and cold stores across three districts. By his second year, Kwabena was earning a steady, dignified income of three thousand five hundred cedis a month, saving in a bank account, and training a younger apprentice of his own.

pages.alt: Certified technician Kwabena installs solar panels on a rural clinic roof alongside Uncle Tetteh and a young apprentice.

pages.text: Two years later, Kwabena was invited to a short, fully funded solar-engineering workshop in Germany through an official embassy visa, and flew back home proudly to expand his Ghanaian workshop! ‘Whether a Ghanaian travels safely across the world or builds right here at home,’ Kwabena told Afia’s JHS class, ‘never gamble your life on a lie. Build real skills, verify the truth, and walk through legal doors with your head held high.’

activities.question: What warning signs showed that the online travel agent’s offer was a dangerous scam?
options: He demanded 35,000 cedis cash, bypassed the embassy, and was unlicensed
He asked Kwabena to study for an accredited electrical exam
He advised the family to check the official government website first
activities.explanation: Demanding large cash payments, promising jobs without official embassy visas, and operating without a licence are major human-smuggling and fraud red flags.

activities.definition: To check whether a claim, licence or document is true and official using reliable sources
distractors: To believe a flashy video on social media without asking questions
To sell family land in secret before Friday

activities.question: How did Cousin Akua’s legal work abroad differ from the smuggler’s false story?
options: She had verified nursing qualifications, an embassy visa and real bills
She travelled without a passport and found money growing on trees
She never had to study or work shifts at the hospital
activities.explanation: Legal migration relies on verified qualifications, contracts and embassy visas, and involves real hard work and living expenses.

activities.question: How much did Kwabena’s family invest in his accredited solar-electrical course (2,500 cedis) and diagnostic tools (2,000 cedis)?
options: 4,500 cedis, saving their cocoa farm and avoiding the 35,000-cedi scam
35,000 cedis in cash to an unregistered stranger
100,000 cedis borrowed from a loan shark
activities.explanation: 2,500 cedis (training) + 2,000 cedis (tools) = 4,500 cedis, keeping the family land safe and building a real career.

activities.prompt: Order the steps that helped Kwabena make a safe, successful life decision.
items: Pause and verify the online agent’s claims with family and official registries.
Listen to honest facts from returnees and legal professionals abroad.
Invest 4,500 cedis in accredited solar training and build a trusted business.

activities.prompt: Why was it important that Maame and Uncle Tetteh treated Kwabena’s frustration with empathy and respect while still protecting him from a dangerous lie?

glossary.definition: Not showing love or support for one’s country (the story explains that migrating safely for work or study is not unpatriotic)
To confirm that information or a licence is genuine by checking official authorities
The official diplomatic office of a foreign country that issues legal visas
Money sent home by a worker living abroad to support their family
Officially recognised and certified as meeting national educational or professional standards
